description:
The Play: Every time you sit down at a restaurant, you think you're in control. You're not. Before you even open the menu, the glasses are already on the table. They hand you a wine list — not a drinks list. And only one person gets it. By the time it makes its way around, the only question anyone's asking is red or white. That's not a choice. That's a corridor they built for you. And here's the kicker — a bottle they paid €6 for just became €30 on your bill. Wine has no price anchor. You don't know what it's supposed to cost. So they charge whatever they want and you'll swear it tastes amazing because you paid for it. The restaurant didn't sell you wine. They just made sure there was nothing else to buy.

The Breakdown: Original curation and breakdown by Market Mojo. What got me about this story isn't the markup — it's how invisible the whole thing is. No pushy waiter. No upsell. Just an environment so carefully engineered that you walk out feeling like you made your own call. That's the most dangerous kind of selling. You never even saw it coming.

The Credit: Weatherbys Private Bank

comments.text:
So this is how you deal with that as a customer, and it's super simple conceptually but it also takes some time and investment:
Go to wine conventions and really try to immerse yourself in it. Wine has this stigma (like many other luxury products) that we think it's better the more expensive it is. That is not true. At my last wine convention, the prices per bottle ranged between 6€ and 15€ (if you buy them in boxes, you often also get a discount). It's not that much because you buy them directly from the source, no intermediary. I found that most wines that I personally liked were in the cheaper price range. I had a 12€ wine that was just completely overwhelming and a 15€ wine that reminded me of the smell of cat piss. Meanwhile, the 7€ wines were often balanced, intense but not overwhelming in flavour and you could imagine them paired with cheese, meat, fish, or certain vegetables depending on the wine.

The most important part imo is learning which grape varieties you like because those influence the taste the most. If you learn that you like a Sauvignon Blanc and dislike a Chardonnay (like me), you already know what to order in most restaurants because most mid-scale restaurants don't carry more than one wine per grape. And then you also have a price anchor because you know that the grape variety you like tends to be a certain price. If the restaurant demands 4x that, you're probably getting fleeced.

Admittedly, writing all of this down, it does sound a tad more complicated than checking out JW Red Label at the supermarket.
